hook: **Five minutes of setup** will save you fifty hours of pain. Let's build your Python workspace the right way — once.

scenes.title: One language. Many versions. Pick **one**.
scenes.sub: Pin a stable release — today that's the 3.13 line
scenes.narration: First decision: which Python? Unlike dot-net's one big SDK, Python has many versions alive at once. Rule of thumb: newest stable for learning, exact same version in production. You can hold several versions side by side, exactly like multiple dot-net SDKs on one machine.

items.s: macOS: brew install python@3.13 — Windows: the official installer

items.t: Switch versions with uv or pyenv
items.s: uv python install 3.13 — modern, fast, written in Rust
Also check pip --version — it should point at the same Python

scenes.narration: Install from python dot org, or Homebrew on a Mac. To juggle versions, use uv — it installs and switches Pythons in seconds. Then verify: run python dash dash version, and check that pip points at the same install. Two Pythons fighting on one path is the classic day-one bug.

scenes.title: Every project gets its **own room**
scenes.sub: venv = your per-project NuGet folder, but stronger
scenes.narration: Now the golden rule. Never install packages into the system Python. Each project gets an isolated environment — its own folder of dependencies. Think of it as a per-project NuGet setup, except isolation is mandatory, not optional. It's called a virtual environment — venv for short.

items.s: Creates a private Python + pip inside your project folder
Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate — your terminal now uses the venv
uv is a 10-100x faster drop-in replacement for pip

scenes.narration: Three commands to remember. First: python dash m venv dot venv — creates a private Python inside your project. Second: activate it — on Mac, source dot venv slash bin slash activate. Third: install packages — and use uv instead of pip when you can. It's the same workflow, ten times faster.

cards.s: Just a list of names. No metadata, loose versions, no build config.
One file: metadata, dependencies, tool config, build rules. The modern standard.

scenes.narration: How do you declare dependencies? The old way is requirements dot text — just a flat list, like a NuGet packages file with no project file around it. The modern way is pie project dot toml. One file holds your metadata, exact dependency rules, and tool configuration. New projects: always pie project dot toml.

items.s: name, version, requires-python, dependencies — the essentials
Pins exact versions — 'works on my machine' becomes reproducible
Ruff, mypy, pytest all configure themselves from pyproject.toml

scenes.narration: Inside pie project dot toml, the project table holds name, version, and dependencies. Add a lockfile — generated by uv lock — and every install is byte-for-byte reproducible, like packages dot lock in dot-net. Bonus: every modern tool reads this same file, so your whole toolchain shares one configuration.

scenes.title: VS Code is **enough** — set it up once
scenes.sub: Debugger + formatter + linter = the Visual Studio trio
scenes.narration: For your editor, VS Code with three extensions covers everything: Python, Pylance for IntelliSense, and Ruff for formatting and linting. The debugger works like Visual Studio's — breakpoints, step over, watch variables. Press F5 and go. PyCharm is the other excellent option if you prefer a batteries-included IDE.

items.s: Type-aware autocomplete and navigation — free Roslyn-style analysis
One blazing-fast tool replacing Black, isort, and a dozen flake8 rules
launch.json once, then breakpoints and stepping like you're used to

scenes.narration: Quick tour. Pylance gives you Roslyn-quality autocomplete and go-to-definition. Ruff is one tool that formats and lints — it replaces an entire stack of older tools and runs in milliseconds. And the debugger needs one small launch dot json, then it's breakpoints and stepping exactly like Visual Studio.

scenes.title: Jupyter: the **scratchpad** for AI work
scenes.sub: Perfect for experiments — wrong place for production code
scenes.narration: Last tool: Jupyter notebooks. A notebook is a page of code cells you run one by one, with results — charts, tables, model output — kept inline. It's the standard way to explore data and test LLM prompts. But remember: notebooks are for experiments. Real code lives in dot-py files.

items.t: Cells run in order — or don't
items.s: Shift+Enter runs a cell; hidden state makes 'run all' a fresh-start test
Build a prompt, call the API, inspect the JSON — all in one page
No git-friendly diffs by default, easy to hide broken state

scenes.narration: How you'll actually use it: write a cell, hit shift-enter, see the result right below. This loop is perfect for prompting an LLM and inspecting the JSON it returns. Two warnings: cells can run out of order, hiding broken state — so always test with run-all from the top. And keep anything reusable out of the notebook and into real files.

scenes.title: Now the language itself
scenes.next: Reel 2 · Syntax Basics — indentation, f-strings, truthiness

recap: Pin one Python version per project; uv or pyenv switches between them
Every project gets its own venv — never install into system Python
Declare dependencies in pyproject.toml + a lockfile; use Jupyter only for experiments

quiz.q: Why does each Python project need its own virtual environment?
opts: So project dependencies stay isolated and reproducible
It's required by the Python license
quiz.why: A venv gives each project its own private set of packages — like per-project NuGet restore folders — so versions never collide between projects.

quiz.q: What's the modern standard file for declaring project dependencies?
quiz.why: pyproject.toml holds metadata, dependencies and tool config in one standard file; a lockfile (uv.lock) pins exact versions.

quiz.q: When is a Jupyter notebook the WRONG tool?
opts: Testing an LLM prompt and inspecting the response
Trying out a library for the first time
quiz.why: Notebooks hide state and don't diff well in git — great for experiments, wrong for code you ship.

code.title: Day-one setup — from zero to a working project
code.body:
# 1. Install a Python version (once)
#    uv python install 3.13

# 2. Create a project + virtual environment
mkdir myproject && cd myproject
uv venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate        # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate

# 3. Declare dependencies in pyproject.toml
#    [project]
#    name = "myproject"
#    requires-python = ">=3.13"
#    dependencies = ["httpx"]

# 4. Install + lock (reproducible!)
uv pip install httpx
uv lock

# 5. Verify which Python you're using
python --version
which python                     # should point inside .venv/
annot: uv venv = python -m venv but faster; both create the same .venv folder
uv lock generates a lockfile so teammates get identical versions
Always check `which python` after activating — wrong interpreter = confusing imports

notes:
# Setup & Tooling

## Python versions
- Many versions coexist; pin **one per project** (`requires-python = ">=3.13"`).
- Install via python.org, Homebrew, or `uv python install 3.13`.
- `python --version` + `which python` are your sanity checks.

## Virtual environments (venv)
- Isolated per-project package folders — **mandatory**, not optional.
- `python -m venv .venv` → `source .venv/bin/activate` → `pip install ...`
- Windows: `.venv\Scripts\activate`.
- **uv** (astral.sh): drop-in pip replacement, 10-100x faster; also manages Python versions.

## Dependency declaration
| File | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `pyproject.toml` | Metadata + dependencies + tool config (the standard) |
| `uv.lock` / `requirements.txt` | Exact pinned versions for reproducibility |

## IDE
- VS Code + **Python** + **Pylance** + **Ruff** extensions.
- Ruff = formatter + linter in one (replaces Black/isort/flake8).
- Debugger: one `launch.json`, then F5, breakpoints, stepping.

## Jupyter
- Cells run individually (Shift+Enter); output stays inline.
- Ideal for data exploration and LLM prompt experiments.
- Pitfalls: out-of-order execution hides broken state; poor git diffs. Keep shippable code in `.py` files.
